pr.title: Check every pull request, license the crate, and add `trip --version`
pr.head: a0ec8154c8ae1627241a7409a06c39c3ec820a7f

summary: trip is a terminal session manager: a daemon owns each session's terminal, and the trip client attaches to it. The releases plan gives it numbered releases, an installer that builds a tagged release from source, and trip upgrade. This pull request is the plan's first step, the bottom of the stack that builds it. It adds the two things every later step depends on: a CI workflow that checks each pull request, and a --version flag that says whether a binary is a release.

Before this change, the repository's only workflow published its project site, so nothing checked a pull request before it merged. And no trip binary could name its version. A release pull request needs passing checks before you merge it, and trip upgrade will compare the version a binary reports with the release tag.

• A version that says whether the build is a release. trip --version and -V print trip 0.1.0 only when TRIP_RELEASE=1 was set at compile time, which the release installer in a later layer will set. Every other build prints trip 0.1.0-dev.
  • Crate metadata and a license. Cargo.toml gains description, license, repository, and rust-version = "1.85", and the repository gains the MIT LICENSE text the README already named.
  • CI. check.yml runs formatting, clippy, the tests, and the end-to-end scripts on every pull request, on pushes to main, and by dispatch, plus a job that checks the build on the minimum Rust version.
  • The plan. releases moves to in-progress and records what implementation settled in a new § 9.

cards.title: Terms
cards.html:
• TRIP_RELEASE: an environment variable read when trip compiles, not when it runs. Only the value 1 marks a release build.
  • MSRV: minimum supported Rust version, the rust-version field in Cargo.toml.
  • workflow_dispatch: a GitHub Actions trigger that starts a workflow on request, on a branch you name.

cards.title: Review so far
cards.html: One Projector review of this head found no blocking problems and suggested three small changes: keep pushes to main from cancelling each other's runs, run the version test with TRIP_RELEASE=0 too, and record the measured CI time in the plan. CI passed on this head: check in 4m 4s and msrv in 23s.

groups.title: trip --version
groups.kicker: A version flag that tells a release build from every other build
intro: trip upgrade, a later step, compares the version an installed binary reports with the release tag, and refuses to touch a checkout install. So the binary has to say both its version and whether it is a release. The release installer will build with TRIP_RELEASE=1 in the environment. trip reads that variable when it compiles, with option_env!, and appends -dev unless it is exactly 1.
Cargo records that the crate read the variable, so changing it between builds recompiles trip. A binary therefore never keeps the answer from an earlier build.

files.note: Adds the VERSION constant and passes it to clap's version attribute, which adds --version and -V.

checks.text: The match compares bytes, [b'1'], instead of the string pattern Some("1"). That is necessary: Rust refuses a str pattern in a constant with E0658, which a test compile confirmed.
Builds of this head print trip 0.1.0-dev with no TRIP_RELEASE, trip 0.1.0 with TRIP_RELEASE=1, and trip 0.1.0-dev with 0 and with 11. Cargo rebuilt trip after each change to the variable.

files.note: Runs the built binary with --version and -V and expects the answer its own build's TRIP_RELEASE calls for. CI runs it once plain and once with TRIP_RELEASE=1.

checks.text: CI runs this test with the variable unset and with 1, but never with another value. So the rule that only 1 marks a release is checked by hand, not in CI.

groups.title: Crate metadata and license
groups.kicker: What a public release needs in Cargo.toml and the repository root
intro: A release needs a license and a stated minimum Rust version. The README's License section already said MIT, but the repository had no LICENSE file. rust-version = "1.85" is the floor because clap 4.6 and vt100 0.18 use Rust's 2024 edition and declare 1.85 themselves. trip's own code needs only 1.82. Setting rust-version also makes clippy flag any standard library API newer than it.

checks.text: The locked clap 4.6.1, clap_builder 4.6.0, and vt100 0.18.1 each declare edition = "2024" and rust-version = "1.85", and CI's msrv job passed on 1.85.

files.note: Documents trip --version and changes the Rust requirement from the 2021 edition to 1.85 or newer.

groups.title: CI on every pull request
groups.kicker: check.yml, the workflow every later step relies on
intro: check.yml runs on each pull request, on each push to main, and by workflow_dispatch. The dispatch trigger exists for the release workflow in a later layer: GitHub starts no workflow for a pull request that a workflow's own token opened, so that workflow will dispatch this one onto the release branch.

1. The check job runs on macOS: cargo fmt --check, clippy with warnings as errors, cargo test, the version test again with TRIP_RELEASE=1, a plain rebuild, and each tests/*_e2e.py script. Each script starts its own daemon in its own temporary home directory.
  2. The msrv job reads rust-version from Cargo.toml, installs that toolchain, and runs cargo check --locked --all-targets.

files.note: New workflow with the check and msrv jobs, read-only permissions, and one concurrency group per ref.

checks.text: The workflow triggers on pull_request, not pull_request_target, grants only contents: read, uses no secrets, and interpolates no ${{ }} expression into a run: step.
cancel-in-progress: true applies to pushes to main too. When two merges land close together, the first merge's run is cancelled, and that commit keeps no check result.
The cargo build --locked after the release-mode test rebuilds target/debug/trip as -dev, because Cargo tracks TRIP_RELEASE. All three end-to-end scripts passed locally against that build.

groups.title: The releases plan
groups.kicker: The plan moves to in-progress and records what step 1 settled
intro: The plan was at ready. Starting its first step moves it to in-progress. Its new § 9 records three decisions: the minimum Rust version and why, that only TRIP_RELEASE=1 marks a release, and that Linux CI stays deferred, as § 7 allowed.

files.note: Changes the status to in-progress and adds § 9, "What implementation settled".

checks.text: § 5 asks for the CI job's time to be measured against a 10-minute budget. The first run on this head took 4m 4s, but § 9 does not record it yet.
